c0006: Equivalent covers per day, year-1 average: about 70 dine-in (sushi bar and tables), about 25 from take-out and pickup (15.6 orders) and about 20 from delivery marketplaces (12.5 orders), counting each order as 1.6 covers. A Friday or Saturday night runs well above the average and a Tuesday well below it (Kit estimate). Compare it with the foot traffic on your street on a Friday night and a Tuesday at lunch
c0008: Per cover, EXCL. sales tax and tip: a dine-in guest spends about $36.00 (food $28.50 plus beverage $7.50); a take-out order averages $41.00 and a marketplace order $46.00 (the menu is about 15% higher there and the order a bit bigger). At 1.6 covers per order, that is $25.60 and $28.75 per cover, and the weighted average of the three channels is $32.48; the example rounds it to $32.50 (Kit estimate). The "Menu price incl. sales tax (calculated)" row below shows the price with your local rate applied
c0010: 365 days minus 52 Mondays (closed) and three holidays: Thanksgiving, Christmas Day and New Year's Day. It is the SAME figure for the P&L, the break-even, the scenarios and the staffing hours
c0014: On year 2. Conservative: the ceiling is set by the sushi bar (10 seats), the 40 seats on Friday and Saturday nights and what the head sushi chef (itamae) and the sushi team can cut
c0022: Cost of goods sold on food sales: about 32%, on the prudent side. Consulting blogs put sushi food cost at 30-40%. The theoretical cost per piece in the Sushi Fish, Rice & Costing Calculator comes out lower (the salmon nigiri and the California roll are cheap, the spicy tuna is not), but the real number is what you buy against what you sell: it also carries fish that goes unsold in the sushi case, trim that is not reused, rice and nori thrown out at close, staff meals, comps and ordering mistakes, and fish prices are Kit estimates. Measure your usage in the first quarter and change this cell
c0024: Beverage cost of about 24% of menu price (Kit estimate): beer, sake and wine are about 70% of beverage sales, and the rest is soft drinks, water and tea. Ask your distributor for the price of sake and beer in writing: sake often depends on an importer
c0026: Sushi trays, soy cups, chopsticks, bags, napkins and wipes for every order that leaves the restaurant, plus containers for leftovers. Local packaging ordinances vary (some cities charge for or ban single-use items): check yours before ordering
c0028: Sales through delivery marketplaces (DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub) with their commission, as a share of total sales. Pickup orders placed directly with you (phone or website) pay no commission and do not go here: push them. Rolls and platters travel well; tempura and gyoza arrive worse, so do not go higher without testing
c0042: About 1,800 sq ft (167 sq m) of second-generation restaurant space with a Type I hood route to the roof possible: a sushi bar counter in view with 10 seats, a 30-seat dining room, a small hot kitchen, a walk-in cooler and a to-go packing station by the door, in a neighborhood with nightlife in a mid-size city (150,000 to 500,000 people), no key money: about $30 per sq ft a year (Kit estimate, editable). The weight of rent on sales is calculated by the workbook itself in the rent row of the "3-Year P&L"
c0046: Gas (rice cookers, fryer, range and griddle), electricity (walk-in, reach-ins, freezer and sushi case, hood and HVAC) and water. The example uses $1,700 per month (Kit estimate). Ask the landlord for the space's utility history
c0048: General liability, product liability (you serve raw fish), liquor liability (beer, sake & wine), property with refrigeration breakdown (spoilage) cover and workers' comp: about $8,000 a year in the example (Kit estimate). Tell your insurance broker you serve raw fish and run a fryer: it changes the premium and the terms
c0061: Interest-only period in years. The example uses 0: principal is repaid from the start. If your lender gives you an interest-only period while you build out, enter it here and check the cash cushion of that year on the "Break-Even" tab
c0063: Three months of fixed costs: the cushion for the opening ramp-up, which with Month 1 in January runs from January to April, when the calendar is also at its slowest
c0072: Rate on alcohol served to go or by delivery. The example uses ONE sales tax rate (8%) for everything, so this cell equals the rate on sales; some states tax food to go or alcohol differently, so check yours. There is no credit for the tax you pay on purchases (see the recoverable input tax cell below)
c0079: Build-out and installations: sushi bar counter, electrical, plumbing, HVAC, Type I hood and exhaust, signage and facade. Ten years straight-line in the example: confirm the tax treatment with your CPA
c0081: Sushi case, rice cookers, freezer, hot-line equipment, walk-in and reach-ins, dish machine, smallwares, furniture and POS: seven years straight-line in the example. Confirm the tax life with your CPA
c0088: Indoor seats: 10 at the sushi bar in front of the sushi case and 30 at tables. Someone who picks up an order or gets it delivered does not take a seat: that is why the seat turns in the row above come out higher than what your dining room really does
c0090: A new sushi restaurant draws curious first-timers in its first month, but regulars and your ratings on the delivery apps take a quarter to build: Month 1 (January) brings in 75% of what it will bring in at month four. With 100% the ramp-up is removed
c0092: Four months to reach cruising speed: January to April
c0094: Two months of rent before opening: the sushi bar build-out, the hood and the permits. If the lender funds the loan when construction starts, add the interest of those months, which this workbook does not count, and remember that any interest-only period starts at signing
c0096: Cushion on the build-out and installations of the space, which is where surprises show up (the hood route, the electrical service for the kitchen, the grease interceptor). A lender will not finance a renovation without one
c0099: Weighted average: dine-in and pickup are paid on the spot, while delivery marketplaces settle weekly what they sell (15% of sales). With weekly payouts that is about 2 days
c0101: Payment terms with the fish, rice, nori and beverage suppliers: what they finance for you. Negotiate it in writing: if your fish supplier asks for weekly payment or COD, lower this figure
c0116: How far projected sales must exceed cash break-even sales (fixed costs plus the loan payment). The drop you can absorb is a bit smaller: with a 15% cushion, 13% of projected sales
c0118: State / local minimum wage; this plan budgets at least $15 per hour for everyone. Enter the full-time annual floor of your state and city if it is higher than the federal one ($7.25 per hour). With 0 the status light compares only against the federal minimum
c0145: Architect, MEP and hood drawings, plan review (Food Code 8-201.11) and permit fees. If you choose a variance for the sushi rice, ask your health department for the plan review fee of the HACCP plan: in some counties it can pass $2,000
c0148: Build-out of a second-generation restaurant space of 1,800 sq ft: sushi bar counter in view, finished kitchen, walk-in room, slip-resistant floors, restrooms (one ADA-accessible), ceilings and acoustic insulation, plus signage and facade. Kit estimate: get two quotes
c0150: Type I hood of about 10 ft with UL 300 fire suppression and makeup air over the tempura fryer, the range and the griddle. Ask the fire marshal and the mechanical inspector in writing what your city requires, and whether the gas rice cookers go under the hood. Installers rarely quote by the foot: ask for an offer with your plans
c0152: Electrical service for the walk-in, the sushi case, the hood and the lighting. Ask what service is available BEFORE you sign: a new service takes time
c0154: Hot and cold water in the kitchen and at the sushi bar, drains with a grease interceptor, HVAC for the dining room and the gas lines for the rice cookers and the fryer
c0156: The case for the neta (the cut fish that goes on top of the rice), in view of the guest and for service only, not for storing fish. A 6 ft Hoshizaki case (70.9 in) lists around $4,045 (read October 2026); the example uses $4,000
c0158: Two commercial gas rice cookers and rice warmers. The hangiri, the wooden tub where the sushi rice is seasoned, goes under smallwares. Kit estimate: ask your equipment dealer for quotes
c0160: The parasite rule (FDA Food Code 3-402.11) asks for raw fish to be frozen at −4 °F or below for 7 days, or at −31 °F until solid plus 15 hours, or at −31 °F until solid plus 24 hours at −4 °F. Tuna and feed-raised aquaculture fish are exempt with a written supplier statement, and records are kept 90 days. This freezer HOLDS the fish you buy already treated, at −4 °F or below with a logger; freezing fish yourself takes a lot of freezer space. Kit estimate: ask for the data sheet
c0162: Fryer for the tempura, range for the miso and stocks, and griddle for the gyoza and teriyaki, all under the Type I hood. Kit estimate
c0164: Walk-in cooler (6×8 ft) for the rice, the vegetables, the sauces and the backup fish stock, with cold holding at 41 °F or below. A 6×8 ft walk-in lists around $12,800 (Norlake Kold Locker, read October 2026)
c0166: Reach-in refrigerators for fish held at 32-34 °F (cold holding is 41 °F or below, and tuna must be received at 40 °F or below), refrigerated prep tables for the sushi bar, a beverage and sake cooler and an ice machine
c0170: Japanese knives (yanagiba and deba), color-coded cutting boards, probe thermometers, scales in oz, the hangiri, the to-go packing station, plateware, allergen signage and the calibrated pH meter (only if you choose a variance for the sushi rice)
c0172: Tables and chairs for 30 seats and 10 stools at the sushi bar
c0174: POS with online ordering, a kitchen display (KDS) or ticket printer, a card terminal and the tablets for the delivery marketplaces
c0176: LLC formation (ask your CPA about LLC vs S corp), EIN and state payroll registration, business license and sales tax permit, building permit and certificate of occupancy, health permit with plan review, and the written food safety plan (a HACCP plan only if you choose a variance). Fees vary by city: replace this line with your own quotes
c0179: Branding, a website with the menu, the consumer advisory and the allergens, a photo session and the opening campaign (Google Business Profile, Yelp, social media)
c0181: Fish (bought already treated or exempt, with the supplier's letter), Calrose sushi rice, nori, sauces, the first order of to-go packaging and the beverages, sake included (order early: it often depends on an importer)
c0215: Sushi, rolls, sashimi, poke, appetizers (edamame, gyoza, tempura), miso soup and desserts: about 67% of sales dine-in, 17% take-out and 15% through delivery marketplaces. One sales tax rate in the example, whether it is eaten at the sushi bar or taken away
c0241: The refrigeration technician for the walk-in, the reach-ins, the sushi case, the rice cookers and the freezer (which must hold −4 °F or below for the parasite records); hood and duct cleaning twice a year (NFPA 96: ask your fire marshal); and the calibration solutions for the pH meter if you use one
c0243: Google Business Profile, social media, photos, the delivery marketplaces' promotions and the peak dates (Valentine's Day, New Year's Eve platters and holiday parties); the opening campaign is in startup costs
c0245: POS subscription (a POS that reports sales tax), online ordering, the delivery tablets, phone and internet
c0249: Trash and cardboard pickup, the grease interceptor service and the used fryer oil, with a licensed waste / grease hauler. Enter the rates of your city
c0255: Certified Food Protection Manager (CFPM) and food handler cards, allergen and raw fish handling training, the renewal of your HACCP plan or variance if you have one, and OSHA basics: knife cuts, fryer and griddle burns, freezer cold and lifting
c0279: Floor for the margin after ALL variable costs (food and beverage, packaging, marketplace fees, card fees and miscellaneous). With about 15% of sales through marketplaces, a sushi restaurant leaves less than a dining room alone. Kit estimate
c0282: Ceiling for cost of goods sold on sales: salmon pays for the menu, while tuna, shrimp and sushi case waste make it more expensive. Kit estimate
c0284: Ceiling for labor on sales with a head sushi chef, a sushi chef and table service at lunch and dinner. Servers' tips go on top and are not part of it. Kit estimate
c0288: Floor for the net result on sales at full pace so the plan holds up. A well-run sushi restaurant earns around 8-11% in this example. Kit estimate
c0320: How far your projected sales exceed cash break-even sales. The drop you can absorb before you cannot pay the fixed costs and the loan payment is a bit smaller: with a 25% cushion, 20%. The minimum required is on the "0. Assumptions" tab
c0322: Full services per seat per day you can run with lunch, dinner and a second dinner turn on Friday and Saturday (stays of 45-60 minutes). It is the physical ceiling of the space, not a target
c0363: Buys from the fish suppliers and files their letters, runs the floor and the delivery marketplaces and manages. In the US the owner is not the one at the sushi bar: you hire the head sushi chef (next row). The workbook imputes a monthly salary as if on payroll, which is the prudent side; confirm with your CPA how you will pay yourself (owner's draw or W-2 under an S corp). The example pays the owner below a manager: owner's draw in addition from net profit
c0365: The head sushi chef (itamae) buys and cuts the fish, runs the sushi bar, signs off the menu, the sushi rice SOP and the parasite records. About $30 per hour in the example. Hire this person before the build-out: it is an investment, not an expense
c0367: The rice cookers, gyoza, tempura, miso soup and teriyaki. About $18 per hour in the example
c0369: Rolls, platters for the delivery marketplaces and the sushi bar when the head sushi chef is off: about $21 per hour (Indeed lists $20.72). With a single person who can cut and build, one absence closes the sushi bar
c0371: Four servers at 0.75 each: dining room, pickup and to-go packing, $15 per hour. Tips go on top and belong to the team
c0373: Part-time W-2 sushi chef for Friday and Saturday dinners and platters made to order: about $20 per hour, never as a 1099 contractor. This plan has NO in-house delivery: if you add it, the driver is a W-2 employee with hired and non-owned auto insurance
c0389: Hours the restaurant is open to the public, adding lunch (11:30-14:30) and dinner (17:00-21:30; 22:00 on Friday and Saturday). The afternoon between the two services is not counted
c0391: Average number of people at the same time across the sushi bar, the hot line, the dining room and the to-go orders. On Friday and Saturday nights you need more: the part-time sushi chef and the extra servers come in (the annual roster does not see them: put them in the shift)
c0393: The day's sushi rice, cutting and cleaning the fish, sauces and mise en place before opening
c0395: The head sushi chef and the line cook. Closing, cleaning and purchasing are outside this schedule: they are the margin between the hours you hire and the hours you need
c0411: 4. All figures are EXCL. SALES TAX. To turn a menu price into a price excl. sales tax, divide it by 1 plus your sales tax rate (a rate of 8% means dividing by 1.08). The example uses ONE rate for everything: dine-in, take-out, delivery and beverages; some states tax food to go or alcohol differently, so check yours. The P&L is excl. sales tax; the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab shows what you actually collect, sales tax included, and the sales tax you remit as a quarterly filer.
c0413: 6. The "12-Month Cash Flow" tab answers the question that decides a bank deal: in which month the cash runs out. Its Month 1 is JANUARY, in calendar order: the opening ramp-up runs from January to April and January is also the slowest month of the calendar, which is why working capital counts. If you open in another month, rotate the seasonality row. The minimum balance of the year can never come out in red.
c0415: 8. The Word business plan in this kit quotes the figures in this Excel: if you change a green cell, the Excel rules. The Sushi Fish, Rice & Costing Calculator is separate: it measures salmon yield and the sushi rice that comes out of each pound of raw rice, and it COSTS each piece by channel. Do not copy the food cost of one nigiri into the "0. Assumptions" tab: the "Cost of goods sold on FOOD sales" cell is the weighted average of the WHOLE menu plus fish waste, thrown-out rice and staff meals, and that is why it comes out higher than the theoretical cost per piece. With the costing of your own menu, check that this average holds.
c0436: In calendar order: the ramp-up falls on January to April, and January is also the slowest month. February (Valentine's Day), May (Mother's Day and graduations) and December (holiday parties) are the peaks. If you open in another month, rotate the seasonality row of the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab

c0440: Consumer demand, not plan buyers. This plan puts 15% of sales through delivery marketplaces

c0447: Kit estimate (Sushi Fish, Rice & Costing Calculator)
